candidates.summary: Cloud platform Northflank reported a security incident and told all users to assume their environment variables have been decrypted and to rotate every secret and credential immediately; multiple users confirmed their AI keys had been used.
facts: Timeline on the status page: Wiz threat alert at 11:43 UTC, initial network policy patch at 12:02 UTC, Wiz CIRT support requested at 13:00 UTC.
13:58 UTC update: 'Assume all environment variables have been decrypted. Disable/rotate all keys.'
15:12 UTC update: secret rotation on Postgres and MongoDB enabled for all users; users told to disable public expose on addons; 'Multiple users are confirming that their AI keys have been used.'
19:28 UTC update: investigation ongoing, no further confirmed findings; guidance unchanged (rotate secrets in workloads, secret groups and global secrets).
At read time the status page listed Networking, Certificates, Services, Addons, Jobs, Builds, and Logs and Metrics as major outage.

candidates.summary: Perplexity CEO Aravind Srinivas shared early evals of Gemini 4 Carbon, calling it the strongest model Perplexity has seen for long-form research and answer quality, with a new state of the art on the Wide-And-Deep-Research (WANDR) benchmark.
facts: He said it is coming to all Perplexity Pro and Max users inside Computer once Perplexity has sufficient token capacity.
The post includes an eval chart image; no scores are given in the post text.

candidates.summary: Drew Breunig baked a working emulator for the NES 6502 CPU into the weights of Qwen3.5-4B, so NES ROMs such as Super Mario Bros run (very slowly) inside the model; he built it with Claude Opus 5.5 and shared the prompts.
facts: Inspired by 'qwenputer' by Divyansh Agrawal.
Breunig's prompt asked Opus to read the qwenputer article and source, explore emulating the NES chip and RAM this way, and build weights plus a CLI that can be pointed at a ROM.
Per Simon Willison, Opus found and used a 15-year-old collection of NES CPU conformance tests by Christopher Pow.

candidates.summary: OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic say they will adopt a shared robots.txt 'policy token' that lets publishers opt out of AI scraping across multiple AI companies at once, instead of setting preferences crawler by crawler.
facts: The signal was proposed at the IETF by Kevin Kelley, a technical lead for standards at Anthropic.
Anthropic has already adopted it; Google and Microsoft plan to support it next year; OpenAI says 'coming months'.
Microsoft will offer separate opt-outs for AI training and AI grounding; sites stay in Bing search results either way.
Meta's Andy Stone signaled support but did not say whether Meta will honor it.

candidates.summary: a16z says a 'Rack Spread' is unfolding: since mid-July GPU rental prices have risen while average token prices fell 58%.
facts: Change since mid-July per a16z: B300 GPU rentals up 106%, B200 up 66%, H100 up 17%, average token prices down 58%.
In the same Charts of the Week, a16z says companies using AI now spend an average of $1,024 per employee on it, nearly 2x last year.

candidates.summary: US tech stocks fell for a second day on concerns about AI spending: Intel dropped 28% on Friday and Alphabet fell another 1.4% after a 12% plunge on Thursday, and the Nasdaq ended October with its worst monthly slide since March 2025.
facts: BBC: Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, Amazon and Microsoft have committed to spending $800bn between them in 2026.

Alphabet lost more than $500bn in market value Thursday after saying AI summaries at the top of search were affecting its core search ad revenue; it expects to spend up to $205bn this year, almost all AI-related.
Intel said it would raise AI spending despite weaker PC demand and does not expect to bring in more cash than it spends this year.
Amazon spent more cash than it made; it has committed $220bn this year.

candidates.summary: Sam Altman said on the Cheeky Pint podcast that, from a global allocation perspective, it is 'quite terrible' for the world's limited DRAM to sit in personal computers for local inference rather than in data centers.
facts: Verbatim per The Verge: "A lot of people want local inference. And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now because we are going to have open-source models, we're going to be able to run them on our computers, and so we're not going to need all the stuff in the data center."
The Verge frames it against OpenAI's buying spree squeezing global RAM supply.
